[§95] On the place of the accented syllable in a Sanskrit word there is no restriction whatever depending upon either the number or the quantity of the preceding or following syllables. sweep_summary: Eleven title hits for Sanskrit (sans1269; catalog = tonal, deciding source Whitney 1889 §§80-96, corroborated by Burrow 1955 and, from the earlier audit, Macdonell 1910/1916, Wackernagel 1896, Kiparsky 2010). Two items were obtained open and read: Bender 1915 (IF 34, archive.org whole-volume scanned) — a corpus count of udātta placement in -mant/-vant derivatives (accent stays on the base except after final-accented i/u/r/-an stems), refining the placement note, silent on pitch vs stress; and Perry & Vaux 2018 (accepted manuscript on Cambridge Apollo) — pitch-mark description (udātta/svarita/sannatara) plus the Kiparsky-Halle Basic Accentual Principle (leftmost underlying accent, else initial), refining placement in the same way as Kiparsky 2010 and consistent with the tonal coding. A Crossref title search also surfaced an open-access 2026 paper not in the target list, Ryan, 'The role of pitch accent in Vedic Sanskrit poetics' (Phonological Data and Analysis 8, CC-BY), fetched sources and read: one accent per word, any syllable, 'tone, not stress', with Rigveda-wide statistics showing the accent is inert in meter — the best new first-hand statement; it confirms rather than supersedes Whitney. Of the rest: Allen 1951 (BSOAS) is Firthian prosody of retroflexion/aspiration (first-page excerpt seen; irrelevant); Mair & Mei 1991 (HJAS/JSTOR) is verse prosody, not word accent (title/Crossref only); Selkirk 1980 (two duplicate Glottolog records; Aronoff & Kean are editors, not co-authors) is prosodic domains/sandhi, no open copy; Janda & Joseph 2002 (De Gruyter, bot-blocked) likely a prosodic-domain critique, unclear and low priority; Katre 1978 (De Gruyter, paywalled; festschrift vol. 3 not on archive.org) on Pāṇini's accent rules, low priority; Kulikov 1997 (print festschrift, no open copy) a note on an accent shift in one verb class, low; Levin 1971 (SUNY Press; archive.org lending-restricted only) comparative, low; Calabrese & Grestenberger 2023 is an unpublished manuscript (Glottolog 'Ms.'), not on LingBuzz or Calabrese's site, medium priority as a modern morphophonological placement analysis. Glottolog author lists for 593927 and 604712 wrongly fold volume editors into the author field. Nothing read contradicts the catalog's tonal coding.

new_statements.quote: In terms of prosodic typology, Vedic is what is commonly known as a pitch accent language, but given that its accent was arguably purely tonal (see below), it could also be called a restricted tone system ... Although I will continue to use the term accent, its phonetic realization should be understood to be tone, not stress. ... Each Vedic word has exactly one accent, with certain well-known exceptions: vocatives, main-clause finite verbs, and certain clitics are unaccented ... Accent is not restricted to a window like it is in, say, Ancient Greek. It can (and frequently does) occur on any syllable of the word, regardless of length.
new_statements.citation: Ryan, Kevin. 2026. The role of pitch accent in Vedic Sanskrit poetics. Phonological Data and Analysis 8, e5: 1-26 (CC-BY 4.0). DOI 10.1017/S2642182825000066.
new_statements.reading: Vedic Sanskrit has a lexically distinctive, culminative (one per word) high-tone accent whose position is free (any syllable, no window, no weight dependence) and which, on the evidence of its total inertness in the quantitative meter of the Rigveda, was realised as tone without stress. This is a first-hand, quantitative, 2026 statement that matches the catalog's 'tonal' coding and Whitney's 'no restriction whatever' on position.

sources.quote: In terms of prosodic typology, Vedic is what is commonly known as a pitch accent language, but given that its accent was arguably purely tonal (see below), it could also be called a restricted tone system ... Although I will continue to use the term accent, its phonetic realization should be understood to be tone, not stress. ... Each Vedic word has exactly one accent, with certain well-known exceptions: vocatives, main-clause finite verbs, and certain clitics are unaccented ... Accent is not restricted to a window like it is in, say, Ancient Greek. It can (and frequently does) occur on any syllable of the word, regardless of length.
sources.locator: p. 1, §1 Introduction (extracted text); conclusion p. 7 (lines 405-417); §1.2.3 Culminativity p. 6
sources.note: Corpus-statistical study of the whole Rigveda (39,833 lines): the lexically distinctive, culminative, privative high-tone accent (udātta) is inert in quantitative meter, which the author takes as evidence that it was tone without concomitant stress ('this article supports Vedic as a language with (largely) culminative tone accent without stress, in which respect it resembles languages such as Tokyo Japanese, Western Basque, and Somali', p. 7). Placement: one accent per word, any syllable, lexically unpredictable in roots. Confirms the catalog's tonal coding and its 'no positional restriction'…

sources.citation: Perry, J. Joseph & Vaux, Bert. 2018. Vedic Sanskrit accentuation and readjustment rules. In Roberto Petrosino, Pietro Cerrone & Harry van der Hulst (eds.), From Sounds to Structures: Beyond the Veil of Maya, 266-294. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. (The Glottolog record lists the three editors as co-authors; the chapter itself names only Perry and Vaux.)
sources.quote: The Vedic texts do not record accent as such. Rather, in manuscripts and critical editions, various pitch features are indicated, from which the placement of the accent can be deduced ... a fall in pitch, known as svarita ('sounded'), and which generally follows the accented syllable, is indicated through a short vertical line above the syllable in question, and a low pitch before the accented syllable, known as sannatara ('more depressed'), is indicated with a horizontal line below the syllable. ... The high-pitched, accented syllable (known as udātta 'raised') is not marked [p. 270]. (7) Basic Accentual Principle (BAP) (as originally formulated by Kiparsky and Halle 1977: 209): If a word has more than one [underlyingly] accented vowel, the first of these gets the word accent. If a word has no [underlyingly] accented vowel, the first vowel gets the word accent. [p. 273]
sources.locator: p. 270 (§2; extracted text) and p. 273, ex. (7) (lines 340-345); accepted-manuscript PDF from Cambridge Apollo, handle 1810/323299
sources.note: Describes the accent as recorded by pitch marks (udātta high, svarita fall, sannatara low) and formalises placement as the Kiparsky-Halle BAP: leftmost underlying (lexical) accent wins, else initial syllable; fixed vs mobile stems (gáv- vs pad-) follow from underlying accentedness of stems and endings; readjustment rules needed for ablaut interactions. Refines the placement rule in the same way as Kiparsky 2010 (already held); consistent with the catalog's pitch-accent coding. The paper uses 'stress' loosely once ('has stress on the stem', p. 273) and in a footnote distinguishes 'accent (conc…

sources.citation: Kiparsky, Paul. 2010. Compositional vs. paradigmatic approaches to accent and ablaut. Author preprint (39 pp) of paper in Jamison, Melchert & Vine (eds.), Proceedings of the 21st Annual UCLA Indo-European Conference. Bremen: Hempen.
sources.quote: '(4) BASIC ACCENTUATION PRINCIPLE (BAP): erase all accents but the leftmost one, and put an accent on the leftmost syllable of an unaccented domain'; word accent is derived from 'the lexically specified accentual features of their constituent morphemes' plus the BAP and an Oxytone Rule for stems; dominant vs recessive suffixes. This is the analysis (Kiparsky 1973/1984, Kiparsky & Halle 1977, Halle & Vergnaud 1987:84, Hayes 1995:297) that StressTyp2 encodes as 'left-most heavy syllable, else initial', where 'heavy' stands for a lexically accented morpheme, not syllable weight; StressTyp2's own
sources.note: Modern formal statement of Vedic accent placement (Basic Accentuation Principle: leftmost lexical accent, else initial); explains that StressTyp2's 'leftmost heavy else initial' is a lexical-accent rule, so the record's 'contra' note can be reworded (not a weight claim) while the TONAL/pitch-accent coding stands.

sources.citation: Macdonell, Arthur Anthony. 1916. A Vedic Grammar for Students. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Appendix III 'The Vedic Accent', pp. 448-469.
sources.quote: 'The Vedic, like the ancient Greek, accent was a musical one, depending mainly on pitch, as is indicated both by its not affecting the rhythm of metre and by the name of the chief tone, udatta raised. That such was its nature is, moreover, shown by the account given of it by the ancient native phoneticians. Three degrees of pitch are to be distinguished ...' Svarita 'is in reality always an enclitic accent following an Udatta'.

sources.citation: Bender, Harold H. 1915. The Accent of Sanskrit -mant and -vant. Indogermanische Forschungen 34: 383-389.
sources.quote: For vocalic stems the following rule is of general application: With a-stems and with stems ending in long vowels (ā, ī, ū) the accent is unchanged. With stems ending in other vowels (especially i and u) the accent is thrown to the suffix, when the last syllable of the primitive bore the accent. Otherwise the accent remains unchanged. This rule applies to both mant and vant. [p. 384] ... The accent remains unchanged in consonantal stems when mant or vant is added, except when vant is added to a stem ending in accented -an; in that case the accent is taken by the vant. [p. 388]
sources.locator: pp. 384 and 388 (scanned lines 19260-19300 and 19607-19640 of the whole-volume djvu text)
sources.note: A corpus count (2200 -mant/-vant derivatives, accented texts only) of where the udātta falls in possessive derivatives: normally on the same syllable as in the base ('primitive'), thrown onto the suffix only after final-accented i/u/r-stems and accented -an stems. Confirms that placement is lexical/morphological (inherited from the base or determined by the suffix), not positional or weight-based; silent on the pitch-vs-stress nature of the accent (it presupposes the accent marks of the texts). Refines the catalog's placement note; does not touch the tonal coding.

But that the Vedic accent was accompanied by some stress is shown by certain phonetic changes which cannot otherwise be explained.'
